item.title: Trump says DOJ will settle remaining Camp Lejeune claims if GOP wins midterms
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
What started as a disjointed speech in Greenville from President Donald Trump ended as a rallying cry from the president to elect struggling Republican candidates on North Carolina’s ballot. Trump went as far as to promise $5,000 to every adult citizen if Republicans take back the House and Senate — a promise he’s made in the past — and to also tie the election results to pending lawsuits by Marines who have suffered serious medical complications from contaminated water at Camp Lejeune. “Tonight, I’m pleased to announce that my administration has delivered $1 billion in cash settlements to these veterans and their families, most of whom are based here,” Trump said. Trump said if Republicans win the House and Senate he will direct the Department of Justice to settle all remaining legitimate claims as soon as possible. “If we don’t win, there’s no money,” Trump said. “If we do win, you’re getting it." Gov. Josh Stein, a Democrat, immediately posted on social media in response to Trump’s statement. “Real leaders fight for the people, not for power,” Stein said. “To condition doing the right thing by sick North Carolinians on who wins the election is foul.” Andrew Bates, a former spokesman for President Joe Biden and an adviser to former Gov. Roy Cooper’s Senate campaign, called Trump’s statement “an anti patriotic thing for the president to say.” Boosting Whatley and bashing Cooper Trump, standing at Pitt-Greenville Airport, told the audience of around 1,500, according to pool reports, that he came to North Carolina for two reasons: “I want to tell you how bad Cooper is, and I want to tell you how great Michael Whatley is.” Cooper, 69, a Democrat from Raleigh, is running against Whatley, 58, a Republican from Gastonia. And Cooper has led every poll since the two men entered the race in July 2025, often by double digits. That’s led key national Republican groups to pull ad funding from Whatley’s campaign and invest in other candidates around the country. And as the rally was underway, news broke that the No Going Back PAC, a super PAC tied to Trump, pulled out of North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District race, Punchbowl News reported. Only North Carolina’s 1st Congressional District, served by Rep. Don Davis, a Democrat from Snow Hill, had originally been expected to be a battleground, and Republican legislators redrew Davis’ district to favor a win for their party. Davis is running against former Trump adviser Laurie Buckhout, a Republican from Edenton. But with Trump’s job approval at an all-time low, and Whatley’s inability to raise his name recognition, despite having led both the state and national Republican parties, there’s been a trickle-down effect to at least five congressional districts among the state’s 14. And that includes the 11th Congressional District, where state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom added her name to the Republican ticket at the last hour after U.S. Rep. Chuck Edwards, a Republican from Flat Rock, withdrew from the race due to a sexual harassment scandal involving congressional employees. Whatley, Buckhout and Balkcom all spoke on stage both before and during Trump’s speech. The same day, the University of Virginia’s Center for Politics changed the 1st and 11th Congressional District ratings from “toss-up” races to “leans Democrat .” Both are in districts that typically are solidly Republican. Republicans hope to ramp up turnout Early Republican turnout was down compared to where it stood in 2022, the last midterm election, according to Western Carolina University political science professor Chris Cooper. State Republican Party Chairman Jason Simmons kicked off Tuesday night’s rally by telling the audience to vote Republican up and down the ballot and to bring friends. “Make sure to go vote, but don’t go alone,” Simmons said. At least one person in the audience said she still hadn’t made up her mind, even about Trump. Maggie Lynn Heron-Heidel, who moved to Tarboro six months ago from Connecticut, write dystopian books and said “there are a lot of people who insist Trump is straight out of a dystopian novel.” She said she hadn’t made up her mind on Trump or his policies so she came to hear him speak. And some of her top concerns were rising costs, especially at the grocery store. Gas prices Trump didn’t address groceries but did talk about gas prices, which have risen as Trump continues a war he started against Iran to stop the country from having nuclear weapons. Trump said Tuesday night, “This is a very small price to pay for keeping a nuclear weapon away from the world’s number one state sponsor of terror.” He promised to lower gas prices again when the war ends. Glenn Mancher, a Merry Hill resident originally from Brooklyn, New York, drove an hour to attend Tuesday night’s rally, wearing a Trump 2028 hat. ”I’d like Trump to finish off the Iranians as quickly as possible,” Mancher said. “That would bring down energy prices.” Bates told McClatchy exclusively that Tuesday’s rally is a “visceral reminder of Michael Whatley’s support for the Iran War that’s making gas and diesel prices skyrocket.” “That’s on top of the unprecedented cuts to health care Whatley wanted, which are hurting people all over Eastern North Carolina just so billionaires like Elon Musk can pay lower taxes,” Bates said. He called Tuesday’s rally “just about the worst message you could take to the Old North State right now.” Crime Trump appeared in North Carolina just 34 days prior and called North Carolina cities “blood-soaked killed fields“ leaning into Republican messaging that Cooper was soft on crime because of the release of more than 3,500 prisoners during the COVID-19 pandemic under a legal settlement. Cooper and other North Carolina officials were sued by civil rights groups during the pandemic after Cooper refused to release half the state’s prison population. A judge told North Carolina officials he’d likely side with the civil rights groups and find that the prison conditions were no longer constitutional because of the virus. To prevent the release of 18,000 inmates, state officials say, they settled and released 3,500. They included DeCarlos Brown on the list of people who were released, despite Brown having already served his full sentence prior to the settlement being agreed upon. But in August 2025, after police said Brown killed Ukrainian refugee Iryna Zarutska on the light rail in Charlotte, Republicans have used the prison release against Cooper’s Senate campaign. On Tuesday, Trump called Cooper “a fool.” “He’s a super liberal fool,” Trump said. “I think a fool, because a senator who cares more about shielding murderers from a cough or a virus or something that will not — for the most part these killers were young, and instead of protecting innocent citizens from bloodthirsty killers — then Roy Cooper is the Dumocrat.” Trump signed into law the CARES Act passed by Congress that allowed the release of more than 13,000 federal prisoners into home confinement during the pandemic. Trump never brought up the CARES Act during Tuesday’s speech but said “it’s crazy” Cooper could become senator after abiding by the court settlement. He and Whatley also questioned Cooper’s mental acuity, a new line of attack from Republicans against Cooper after The North State Journal published a cease-and-desist demand from the Cooper campaign in response to a reporter from the outlet questioning whether he had a “neurological issue.” Cooper’s lawyers said Cooper does not, and that to publish anything to the contrary would be defamatory. Trump turned his attention to Whatley, crediting him for the success of Trump’s 2024 campaign. At the time, Whatley was leading the Republican National Committee. “A lot of people said it’s one of the best campaigns ever run,” Trump said. “I wanted him to be the guy, and I was right. I called it right. And I think he’ll be an even better senator.” Trump handpicked Whatley to succeed Sen. Thom Tillis, a Republican from Huntersville, who got into a public feud with Trump over how Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill would affect North Carolina’s Medicaid recipients. That caused Tillis to drop his reelection bid, and Trump to tap Whatley to run against Cooper. Trump’s visit Tuesday night came one day after the vice president traveled to Hendersonville for a similar rally, and exactly two weeks before the election. Trump said he will likely come to the state again before Nov. 3. This article originally appeared on Raleigh News and Observer at https://www.newsobserver.com/news/politics-government/election/article317709089.html

item.title: Trump says the economy is booming. Vance says there's more work to do.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Bill Clinton famously said he could feel voters’ pain over the economy. But these days, when it comes to questions about high prices , President Donald Trump insists that the pain is his. “They hit me with affordability, and that’s the first time I ever heard the word used,” he complained in Nebraska earlier this month. The White House leaves Vice President JD Vance to use a softer touch. Last month in Texas, he admitted “there are people out there who are frustrated by the pace of progress." And during a CBS News town hall on Saturday, Vance said, “I recognize that gas prices are too high right now" and "we’re working on it.” Depending on which Republican is speaking, Americans are getting a different perspective on how bad things are with the economy. Trump says “the golden age of America is upon us.” Vance walks a tightrope to show that he knows voters are feeling an economic pinch while still selling them on Trump's agenda. The disconnect comes as Americans’ confidence in the economy sank to the lowest level in more than a decade this month, the average long-term U.S. mortgage rate jumped this month to its highest level in nearly three years and the unemployment rate ticked up last month . Recent economic data released this month shows that high gasoline prices are intensifying inflation and more expensive oil and gas have begun to push prices up in other parts of the economy. While most of Trump's supporters don't hold him at fault, some acknowledge that the president's penchant for salesmanship may not hit the mark. "I think he talks it up,” said Conda Little, a 76-year-old retiree who went to see Trump in Dalton, Georgia, on Friday. “I think Vance is more real.” Little takes the president at his word that he will achieve a victory over Iran in a way that benefits U.S. consumers back home. But she said it’s impossible to deny the fallout from the conflict. “Everybody’s real upset about the gas” and “groceries are out of sight,” she said. “It’s hard. It’s really hard,” she said, adding that, “I think that people need to hear the truth.” ‘We need to do more’ Trump is loath to acknowledge concerns. He told reporters earlier this month that he gives himself “an A+ on the government, on economics, on everything.” He has dismissed concerns about high costs, arguing that concerns about affordability are a “hoax.” “We’re in the golden age of America. So our nation is doing better now than ever before,” he told a crowd in Kentucky on Saturday while campaigning for Republican candidates. Trump has occasionally acknowledged that gas prices are high , but has called it “a small price to pay” for keeping the country and the world safe with the Iran war. Trump’s discordant message with one of the top concerns voters are voicing ahead of the midterm elections has seemed heightened by his fixation on beautifying Washington and building a large ballroom at the White House. During a visit this month to an economically struggling corner of Arizona, he regaled the crowd with the story about how he ended up with a luxury jet gifted by Qatar to use as Air Force One. Vance, as he crisscrosses the country, is quick to say that the administration has more work to do. To cast blame, the vice president often says that his administration’s Democratic predecessors put the country in such a deep hole that they need more time to climb out. To show empathy, he often references his own experience growing up in a working-class family in a Rust Belt town. That's far different from Trump, who comes from a wealthy family, is a billionaire and even joked during his speeches on Friday and Saturday that if people have lunch at his Mar-a-Lago club, "for $5,000, you’ll get one hamburger and a small dessert.” Vance, during a CBS News town hall that aired on Saturday, said: “I grew up in a working-class family. When gas prices were high, I know that it made my grandmother suffer, and I’m sure that you’re struggling with it in a variety of ways." When asked by the moderator about the mixed message he and Trump are giving on the economy, Vance said Trump was speaking about new investments coming into the country, but said the changes take time. “We need to do more, and we can certainly do better,” he acknowledged. Many Trump supporters trust his pitch Some voters said Trump’s rosy view on the economy turns them away, like Santiago Rodriguez, a 19-year-old Texas college student who will be voting for the first time this year. Rodriguez, who attended a campaign rally last week for Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico, said he would consider voting for a Republican but not while Trump is in charge because he doesn’t grasp the high cost of living for Americans. “I think he’s out of touch, I think he’s never seen what a true day as a Texan or anybody in general who is in the working class,” Rodriguez said. Trump's most loyal supporters aren’t interested in blaming high prices on anything the president has done. Cindy Massengill, a 67-year-old who came to see Trump in Dalton, Georgia, said she felt he’s doing the best he can. “I’m positive that he’s got done more than any other president after the mess we were left with Obama and Biden,” she said. Mary Bunker, a 67-year-old Republican who attended Trump’s Monday rally near Wichita, Kansas, said she works multiple jobs, including as a waitress and DoorDash driver. She feels the pressure of high gas prices, but she likes the tax breaks that Trump signed into law last year and she doesn’t fault the way he speaks about economic concerns. “I think he’s a very good businessman,” Bunker said. “He’s been in business a long time, so I think he knows what he’s talking about.” ___ Associated Press writers Bill Barrow in Dalton, Georgia, Jesse Bedayn in San Marcos, Texas, and Nicholas Ingram in Park City, Kansas, contributed to this report. This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/golden-age-vs-were-working-040104930.html

item.title: Armed federal agents knock on doors looking for noncitizen voters
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Armed and in uniform, federal agents from the Department of Homeland Security have been knocking on doors in several states to ask residents about their immigration status — and to inquire if they have registered to vote or cast votes in past elections, a CBS News Investigation has found. The operation is part of an effort to root out potential noncitizen voters ahead of the midterms. DHS has alleged that there could be as many as 250,000 citizens illegally registered to vote, although election experts have disputed the accuracy of this figure. Just 156 people have been charged with voting-fraud related offenses since the beginning of the Trump administration, according to the Department of Justice. There are 227 million registered voters in the U.S. Critics say that sending armed federal agents to the doors of U.S. residents could be intimidating for legal voters. "What we're seeing now is the federal government is inserting itself into the state process for verifying their voter roles in an unprecedented way," said Jessica Marsden, a lawyer for Protect Democracy, a left-leaning advocacy group that is suing the federal agency over the door-knocking campaign. "And they are doing it in a way that seems maximally designed to scare lawful voters from participating." The home visits ramped up in September, in the thick of the midterm campaign season, and continued over the past weekend. The Justice Department announced Monday that Homeland Security agents in California arrested more than 20 people , all of them green card holders , on allegations they had illegally registered or cast a vote. As part of that roundup, dozens of federal agents descended on the residence of a 72-year-old man from Belize, who was taken from his home in his pajamas and arrested on charges he allegedly voted illegally in the past four elections. "HSI is actively rooting out and investigating election fraud wherever it can be found," said a DHS spokesperson. "Under President Trump, HSI is committed to restoring integrity to our election systems and ensuring that American citizens and only American citizens are electing American leaders." Eric Balliet, a former Homeland Security Investigations agent, said the door-knocking operation is a significant departure from traditional law enforcement activities. "In my 23 years with HSI, I never engaged in or was aware of any incident of initiative that sent Special Agents to private residences to verify the eligibility of voters," Balliet said, who served in the federal government under multiple administrations. In June, the DHS directed U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, to assist in deportations of alleged noncitizen voters. Homeland Security Investigations, the agency conducting the at-home visits, is one of the enforcement arms of ICE and typically focuses on criminal cross border investigations like child exploitation, drug smuggling and money laundering. Months later after the announcement, hundreds of agents were pulled off their cases and assigned to track down alleged noncitizen voters as part of a "surge" initiative, according to internal documents reviewed by CBS News. The directive, first reported by CNN , describes a "Criminal Voter Fraud " initiative that includes "field reviews" in at least six states including California, Georgia, Missouri, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin. Photos and videos posted on X show agents from Homeland Security Investigations, some of whom are carrying firearms , approaching houses and knocking on doors, under captions like, "AMERICAN ELECTIONS ARE FOR AMERICANS." One photo from Kansas City HSI's account shows four agents at the door of a woman standing on her porch holding a child's hand. The woman is identified in a Department of Justice press release as Mariana Alexandra Dewey, a Peruvian national who was charged with four counts of voter-fraud related crimes including illegally casting a ballot in the 2024 election. Her case has not yet been heard. Her lawyer declined to respond to CBS News' request for comment. For civil rights advocates, the show of force has sparked concerns about the chilling effect it could have on legal voters. "It is sending the signal to a much broader community, do not show up at the polls. Do not vote," said Dr. Carol Anderson, a professor of African American Studies at Emory University. "And so if you are somebody who has registered to vote and you're a naturalized citizen, what you see in that community is that — because this is not a regime that makes those discernments — that you're gonna stay away from the voting booth." A DHS spokesperson said, "DHS and DOJ are laser focused on prosecuting and removing aliens who vote and preventing the dilution of the votes of U.S. citizens… Those who are here legally and are not breaking other laws have nothing to fear." "Target List" In one video, agents are filmed holding a document that says, " Target List ." That list can be far reaching, said a HSI agent familiar with the initiative who asked to speak anonymously. DHS pulls from internal databases, voter rolls, and other datasets. Then employees attempt to match names against citizenship data provided by the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, or USCIS. In September, a USCIS whistleblower said that employees were asked to review the voter information of tens of thousands of individuals across the country, including citizens. Employees were given quotas to investigate 40 subjects a day, which is a rate of roughly 12 minutes per subject. DHS has defended the data matching program and the work USCIS has done to identify potential noncitizen voters. "Far from being rushed or untrained, these investigative efforts are conducted diligently and professionally," said a DHS spokesperson. "There is no quota on criminality. DHS will pursue each and every illegal voter to the fullest extent of the law ." "There's every reason to expect that there are many, many more false positives in these lists," said Marsden. She noted that Homeland Security officials initially said they had identified nearly 16,000 noncitizens on Nevada's voter rolls, but ultimately they were unable to provide evidence of a single illegally registered voter. This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/federal-agents-seek-noncitizen-voters/

item.title: Democrats sue Trump over efforts to remove voters from rolls ahead of midterms
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Democrats have filed a lawsuit against President Donald Trump and the Justice Department, alleging that the Trump administration is unlawfully interfering with the midterms by pressuring states to remove voters from their rolls. The complaint, filed Tuesday in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, cites the Department of Homeland Security’s recent demands that states remove alleged noncitizens from their voter rolls. The complaint argues such action is based on “shoddily compiled lists” that have “crumbled upon the barest inspection.” Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. The complaint also alleges that Trump administration officials at the Justice and Homeland Security departments have directed a “persistent stream of threats and intimidation” at state and local election officials across the country. The complaint noted that Trump himself had last week threatened to imprison California election officials if they counted mail-in ballots by people the Trump administration claimed were noncitizens. “None of this is lawful,” the complaint states. “The Executive Branch enjoys no authority to superintend state voter list maintenance, to supplant state determinations of who is qualified to vote, or to dictate who gets a ballot or whose ballot gets segregated.” The complaint, filed by three national Democratic groups and other Democratic leaders, asks a federal court to stop Trump and his administration from trying to alter states’ voter rolls and to stop pressuring and threatening election officials. In a statement Wednesday, the Justice Department said that enforcing federal election law and election integrity was a top priority. “Every action the Department has taken to protect the integrity of this year’s elections is grounded in the law and being litigated in open court. Ensuring that only eligible citizens vote and that every lawful ballot is counted a requirement of federal law,” Justice Department spokeswoman Kiersten Pels said. Asked about the lawsuit Wednesday, White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis blamed Democrats for fighting “common sense election-security measures.” “Anyone who illegally votes in our elections will be held accountable,” Bis said in an email. Trump has spent years claiming noncitizen voting is rampant, even though court reviews and independent studies have found it is rare. Many of the administration’s claims of noncitizen voting have fallen apart under scrutiny. This summer, the Department of Homeland Security asserted that up to 16,000 voters on the rolls in Nevada could be noncitizens. It later dramatically scaled back its claims and provided the state with a list of 185 suspected noncitizens. State officials checked those names and determined all of them were citizens. Earlier this month, the Justice Department sued California officials over what it claimed were more than 20,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls. California elections officials have also said those numbers are not accurate. A preliminary review of a sample of 200 of those voters found more than half were not sent ballots and many appeared to be eligible to vote, according to filings from the Registrar of Voters office in Los Angeles County. The complaint filed Tuesday was made by the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, the Democratic Governors Association, the Nevada Democratic Party, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-New York), House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-New York) and Erick Jose Jimenez, a naturalized citizen and California resident. In addition to Trump and the Justice Department, the complaint also names Attorney General Todd Blanche, the Department of Homeland Security and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin as defendants. The legal challenge comes one day after elected officials in a Northern Virginia county also sued the Trump administration, alleging that administration officials have unlawfully claimed the authority to send armed federal agents to polling places. The lawsuit, filed in federal court Tuesday by the Arlington County Board, alleges that the administration’s policies threaten to disrupt the voting process and undermine trust in local election officials. The lawsuit said the potential for federal interference has forced county officials to “plan for and expend resources to address the possibility of unlawful activity and the reasonable fears of voters and election workers.” “Threatening to send armed agents to polling stations is unlawful and contravenes the bedrock values of free and fair elections we hold dear in this country,” Matt de Ferranti, chair of Arlington County’s board, said in a statement. “These statements are a clear attempt to stoke fear and undermine confidence in our elections.” Liam Bowman contributed to this report. Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/10/21/democrats-sue-trump-doj-over-effort-remove-voters-state-rolls/

item.title: House Republicans face a constitutional test after agents seize Ilhan Omar's phone
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
House Republicans have publicly cheered on the Trump administration’s investigation of Rep. Ilhan Omar. But underneath the posturing, the raid raises thorny nonpartisan questions about how aggressively Congress wants to defend itself from encroaching federal prosecutors. The Department of Homeland Security investigators who raided Omar’s Washington home last week were searching for evidence related to the Minnesota Democrat’s immigration history. But they also emerged in possession of her personal phone, which likely includes a trove of records related to Omar’s work at the Capitol — records that both parties have a strong interest in keeping private. Lawmakers use their cellphones and computers to communicate with aides about upcoming votes, committee hearings and drafting or filing legislation. They text and email colleagues about the work of the House. And they talk to constituents, advisers, attorneys and experts about crucial congressional decisions. The Constitution’s “speech or debate” clause makes such material absolutely immune from scrutiny by federal prosecutors, with few exceptions. The founders adopted those protections to ensure the executive branch could not use its law enforcement power to punish or coerce opponents in Congress. That principle has united Democrats and Republicans, even in this hyperpolarized era. Speaker Mike Johnson has yet to weigh in on the speech-or-debate implications of the Omar raid, but the House has sometimes taken weeks or months to articulate a position in other recent investigations. A letter from Omar’s attorneys to the Justice Department, reviewed by POLITICO, suggested that the magistrate judge who approved the search ordered investigators to contact the House’s top lawyer, Matthew Berry, giving him a chance to intervene on behalf of the institution. Berry’s office has been in contact with Trump administration counterparts in recent days, according to two people familiar with the investigation. The people, who were granted anonymity because they are not authorized to discuss the probe publicly, say investigators have not yet accessed Omar’s phone. If they choose to attempt to access it, they must first give Omar a chance to review its contents and assert speech-or-debate protections, with a court ultimately deciding which materials investigators may access. A representative for the Justice Department declined to comment. Representatives for Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Johnson and Omar did not respond to requests for comment. The administration’s targeting of Omar comes amid a series of actions the Trump-led Justice Department has taken against Democratic members of Congress: a failed effort to indict Sens. Mark Kelly of Arizona and Elissa Slotkin of Michigan, along with several House members, over comments encouraging members of the military to refuse unlawful orders and criminal charges against Rep. LaMonica McIver for allegedly assaulting an ICE officer during a visit to a New Jersey detention facility. It also comes amid continued GOP outrage over former special counsel Jack Smith's decision to gather some material related to Republican members of Congress in the aftermath of the 2020 election. The House’s official legal positions are determined by an obscure five-member body known as the Bipartisan Legal Advisory Group, or BLAG. The BLAG is made up of the speaker, majority leader, majority whip, minority leader and minority whip. That panel, always controlled by the majority party, charts the House’s course in court. And while most of the BLAG’s recent decisions have broken 3-2 along partisan lines, speech-or-debate issues have sometimes resulted in unanimous agreement. Berry has seen this movie before: In 2022, federal investigators seized the phone of Rep. Scott Perry (R-Pa.) to scrutinize his role in President Donald Trump’s bid to subvert the 2020 election. The Justice Department’s aggressive action drew a bipartisan response from House leaders, who demanded access to the sealed proceedings to ensure prosecutors didn’t cross any constitutional lines. And shortly after Republicans returned to the majority in 2023, Jeffries and Minority Whip Katherine Clark joined GOP leaders and supported Berry’s filing of a 36-page brief demanding robust protection of materials seized from lawmakers’ cellphones. That case resulted in a new precedent that treats lawmakers’ personal cellphones as an extension of their private offices. It took more than a year of litigation before those investigators, later led by Smith, were able to access a subset of Perry’s records that were deemed to fall outside of Congress’ constitutional protections. Stan Brand, a former House counsel who represented Perry in the legal battle against Smith’s team, noted that the backdrop of the Omar situation is strikingly similar to one of the most significant constitutional clashes between the House and Justice Department: the 2006 raid of then-Democratic Rep. William Jefferson’s congressional office by George W. Bush-era prosecutors. At the time, GOP House leaders joined Democrats in outrage over the raid. Notably, the DHS investigators who carried out last week’s search presented Omar with a “speech or debate” waiver that she refused to sign, according to the letter from Omar’s attorneys. Courts have expressed skepticism about whether individual members can waive protections that were intended to safeguard the separation of powers for the entire institution. “This is just one more example of excess in the Department of Justice under both Democrats and Republicans,” Brand said. Senate Republicans have also accused the Justice Department under President Joe Biden of violating their speech-or-debate protections when Smith subpoenaed their phone records — which don’t include the content of texts or emails — from third-party telecom companies like Verizon. One GOP senator is suing Smith and the Justice Department over the matter, and DOJ has since adopted new policies for third-party subpoenas related to members of Congress. Riley Rogerson and Mia McCarthy contributed to this report. This article originally appeared on Politico at https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/21/ilhan-omar-investigation-house-01128174

item.title: Meta ordered to pay $25 billion after jury finds company liable for deceiving users
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Diana Novak Jones Oct 21 (Reuters) - A judge in New Mexico ordered Meta Platforms to pay $25 billion on Wednesday after a jury found the company had misled consumers in a case arising from allegations that a political consulting firm involved in Donald Trump's 2016 presidential campaign obtained data from millions of Facebook users without their consent. New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said it was one of ‌the largest, if not the largest, single state verdict against the company in American history. "Facebook's wrongdoing — over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public — goes to the heart of Facebook's core business ‌practices," Judge Francis Mathew wrote in his order following the verdict. Mathew found that a penalty of more than $219 billion was warranted, based on state law, but he reduced the figure to $25 billion. In a statement, C.J. Mahoney, Meta's chief legal officer, said the company is confident it will win ​on appeal. “This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Mahoney said. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online." The company had previously said a penalty in the billions of dollars risked violating its constitutional rights to due process and protection from excessive fines. The penalty is the largest levied against the tech giant in the wake of the Cambridge Analytica scandal. In 2019, the company was hit with a $5 billion penalty by the US Federal Trade Commission stemming from the same scandal. Six other states settled their lawsuits related to Cambridge Analytica for $459.2 million as part of a $17.1 ‌billion multistate settlement Meta reached in August to resolve states' claims that the company's ⁠platforms had harmed teen mental health. LAWSUIT FILED FIVE YEARS AGO New Mexico's attorney general had sued Meta in 2021 following revelations that Cambridge Analytica had harvested personal data from as many as 87 million Facebook users through a third-party app. The state accused Meta of lying to Facebook users in New Mexico about who had access to their data, how the company handles ⁠hate speech and misinformation posted on the platform and other internal policies. The company knew that third parties had broad access to users' personal data, and it tolerated hate speech or other harmful content when it benefited the company's bottom line, the state said. Cambridge Analytica, now defunct, worked for Trump's successful presidential campaign in 2016, and gained access to the personal information from millions of Facebook accounts for the purposes of voter profiling and targeting. It obtained that information without users' consent from a researcher who had been ​allowed ​by Facebook to deploy an app on its social media network. "It has been a long time coming holding Big Tech accountable," Torrez told ​a press conference in Albuquerque after Wednesday's ruling. "I think today's judgment is a clear break ‌with that past and a very clear warning to those in this space and beyond that we intend to protect our people and protect our consumers." Analyst Gil Luria, head of technology research at D.A. Davidson & Co, called the ruling costly but unlikely to impact the company's value. "Meta is worth nearly two trillion dollars, and will likely continue to appeal these cases and drag them out," Luria said. EXPERTS EXPECT LONG APPEAL FIGHT Legal experts and financial analysts said the penalty was likely to face a lengthy battle on appeal. Jurors on September 25 found that 26 of 29 statements made by the company and its leadership on those issues were misleading. They said the company had committed more than 43 million violations of New Mexico’s consumer protection laws, based on the number of Facebook users or New Mexico residents who were the audience for each misleading statement. State law allows a penalty of up to $5,000 per violation, and directs that all of the ‌money go to New Mexico's school system, Torrez told reporters after the verdict. At a hearing on October 1, Randi McGinn, a lawyer for ​New Mexico, had asked Mathew to award the state between $35 billion and $40 billion, saying that would be supported by the US Constitution's protections ​on due process and the jury's verdict. "This court should speak to Meta in the only language it understands, ​which is money, and the value of its stock price," McGinn said. In court filings, Meta urged Mathew to cap the penalties at $3.45 billion, saying a higher penalty ran the risk of ‌scaring businesses out of the state. The evidence showed that Meta does not sell ​user data and New Mexico did not prove that any consumer ​had actually been misled, the company said in court filings. Daryl Lim, an associate dean at Penn State Dickinson Law, said that while the US Constitution generally protects against excessive fines, because of the way New Mexico law is written, the large size of the penalty does not automatically mean it could be overturned. TWO JURIES SIDED WITH STATE The verdict was the second in six months by a Santa Fe jury in a ​lawsuit brought by the state of New Mexico against Meta Platforms. In the first trial, ‌which ended in March, a Santa Fe jury found Meta misled users about young users’ safety on its Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp platforms and ordered the company to pay $375 million in civil penalties. After ​a second phase of that trial, a judge directed the company to pay $567 million into a New Mexico fund for teen mental health and ordered Meta to implement measures to protect teen ​Facebook and Instagram users in New Mexico. (Reporting by Diana Novak Jones, Editing by Alexia Garamfalvi, Nia Williams and Aurora Ellis) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://finance.yahoo.com/news/meta-ordered-pay-25-billion-172737485.html

item.title: Ramaswamy doubles down on ad of Acton's estranged mother with $4 million buy
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy is doubling down on a controversial ad featuring his opponent's estranged mother with a $4 million buy. The ad, which leaked Oct. 19, features the estranged mother of Democratic candidate Amy Acton accusing the candidate of lying about her upbringing. Acton hasn't spoken to her mother since 1978, when her stepfather, Cledith Arthur, was accused of sexually abusing her as a child. Acton's brother, Philip Stearns, and court records reviewed by the statehouse bureau back up Acton's account of a childhood filled with abuse, neglect and at times, homelessness. Acton's mother, Donna Arthur, lost custody of her two children and left Ohio with Cledith before the rape case against him could be resolved. “It’s not surprising that Vivek Ramaswamy has stooped to such a despicable low as to attempt to turn the sexual abuse Amy endured at 12 years old from our birth mother's husband into a political talking point,” Stearns said. But Ramaswamy is airing that ad anyway. The Republican candidate said people close to Acton, including a mother she has not spoken to in 48 years, have urged Ohioans not to vote for her. "This is part of a pattern of someone else who appears to know her well who says the same thing, and I do think that it's important for voters to take all of that into account," Ramaswamy told the statehouse bureau. More: Ramaswamy confirms ad featuring Acton's estranged mother is from his campaign What is the ad? The ad features Acton's estranged mother, Donna Arthur, urging voters not to pick Acton for governor. "If you think she'll make your life better, you're fooling yourself," Arthur said in a 60-second ad cut by the Ramaswamy campaign. Ramaswamy said Acton's mother wasn't paid to appear in the spot. The ad is at least the second time Arthur has publicly accused her daughter of lying. Arthur detailed concerns about Acton's backstory to an anti-abortion group in 2020 while Acton was serving as state health director. Ramaswamy's campaign confirmed it will spend $4 million on the spot before Election Day, Nov. 3. More: Criticism grows over attack ad featuring Amy Acton's estranged mother What does the record show about Acton's childhood? Acton detailed her troubled home life and her mother's neglect in a Youngstown Vindicator article published in August 2019. She described living in "18 or so" homes, including one unfinished basement, before turning 12. She recalled Arthur's many boyfriends and their frequent moves. At one point, they lived in a tent outside of Youngstown, Acton told the Vindicator. According to Acton, the situation escalated when her stepfather sexually abused her at age 12. Austintown Police arrested Cledith Arthur in summer 1978 for the rape of a 12-year-old girl "following an investigation initiated by the girl's father," the Youngstown Daily Vindicator reported at the time . Cledith Arthur left the state before the case could be resolved. A warrant was issued for his arrest in October 1978 and December 1981, according to court records provided to the statehouse bureau. A records request has been filed with the Mahoning County Common Pleas Court, and they are working to pull records on the case from 1978. In a campaign video last week, Stearns verified Acton's account of their upbringing. "I received a lot of abuse, but Amy always got the worst of it. She continued to receive that abuse because she knew she had to protect me from that, and if she hadn't done that, who knows where I would have ended up," Stearns said. How did Acton respond? Acton's campaign launched a response ad featuring her brother talking about how Acton protected him during their difficult childhood. Acton also addressed the ad on her social media: "Growing up in Youngstown, my brother Phil and I endured abuse, hunger, and neglect − even spending one winter homeless living in a tent. We were often kept in a dark basement, were frequent-fliers with child protective services, and lived in fear of our birth mother’s violent and erratic temper," Acton said in a statement. "Between the ages of 10 and 12, I was sexually abused by her husband, while my birth mother did nothing to protect me. I’ve always known that she was deeply sick and unwell, and it’s sad to see Vivek Ramaswamy exploit her all for his own political gain." "Eventually, I confided in my father and stepmother, and we were removed from that situation. My birth mother’s husband was arrested, charged with rape, and indicted by a grand jury. At 12 years old, I testified in court. I haven't seen my birth mother since that day in 1978. She and her husband fled the state and he was declared a fugitive," she wrote. State government reporter Jessie Balmert can be reached at jbalmert@usatodayco.com or @jbalmert on X . item.title: Who cut Ukraine's Starlink speeds? White House and Musk offer conflicting accounts.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Wednesday pushed back against suggestions that the Trump administration had ordered Elon Musk’s Starlink and its military-grade counterpart, Starshield, to limit Ukraine’s access to the satellite communications networks, saying any such decisions were up to the SpaceX founder — and not the White House. “We cannot direct a private company as to the decisions they make or not make,” Rubio told reporters on an overseas trip in Mumbai. Rubio had stated previously that “nobody” had ordered Starlink’s speed to be slowed down, adding that it just “sort of happened.” The secretary of state spoke by phone with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Tuesday in an effort to ease tensions. Appearing on Fox & Friends on Wednesday, Zelensky said that Starlink connectivity is still limited in Ukraine and was told by Rubio that the U.S. State Department would work to “unblock” the slowdown. What is Starshield and why is it so important to Ukraine? Ukraine soldiers set up a Starlink satellite communication terminal in the Donetsk region on Oct. 16. NurPhoto via Getty Images Starshield is a low-earth satellite network designed by SpaceX for government use. According to SpaceX , Starshield "leverages Starlink technology and launch capability to support national security efforts." The Ukrainian military has been using the system for communications between its armed forces, allowing Kyiv to carry out drone strikes against Russia. Earlier this month, officials in Kyiv said they discovered that Ukraine’s access to Starshield had been throttled by SpaceX, limiting its ability to defend itself from Russian ballistic missile attacks on energy infrastructure. The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday that Musk ordered the slowdown after discussions with President Trump about Ukraine’s recent attacks on Russia’s diesel refineries, which Trump has blamed for skyrocketing U.S. fuel prices. Elon Musk speaks at the 2020 Satellite Conference and Exhibition in Washington. ASSOCIATED PRESS “Musk capped the speeds at which Ukrainian hardware could stay connected to the satellite-based network,” the Journal reported, “rendering some offensive drones and interceptor drones virtually useless.” Last week, the Telegraph reported that Musk has approached Trump with “the idea of slowing down Starlink in Ukraine," and that Trump "agreed." In a post on X , Musk said Starshield systems are “owned and controlled by the US government” and that “any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS." Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS. Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities… — Elon Musk (@elonmusk) October 14, 2026 In response, Trump denied any involvement , saying: "I don't know if it was anybody, but it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon." On Wednesday, Rubio insisted that neither the president nor anyone in the administration “ever requested that any changes to that system be made.” But he would not say whether the United States was aware of the decision to limit Ukraine’s access to Starshield beforehand. “I’m not going to comment on what we knew that they might or might not do,” Rubio said. “The president has nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr. Musk,” the secretary continued. “That’s a private company. The president doesn’t run that company and can’t direct that company to do anything.” He added: “I’m telling you there was no foreknowledge, but beyond it, even if there was, we don’t control what a private company — how they decide their product can be used.” Rubio: If not for U.S., ‘there would be no Ukraine right now’ A young woman reacts as she looks at her damaged home after a Russian missile attack in Kyiv on Oct. 14. Efrem Lukatsky/AP The secretary also took issue with comments by Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, one of Ukrainian Zelensky’s military advisers, who told the BBC that U.S. intelligence had also failed to give Ukraine advance warnings of incoming Russian ballistic missile strikes, resulting in the deaths of civilians. “I don’t know who this official was in the Ukrainian Government that went around saying that a bunch of people had died as a result of what America was denying them,” Rubio said. “No country in the world has done more to help Ukraine over the last four and a half years than the United States, including under the Trump administration, and that continues to be the case.” He added: “We’re no longer going to be defensive about this topic, OK? Because if it were not for the assistance of the United States, including under the Trump administration, there would be no Ukraine right now.” This article originally appeared on Yahoo News at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/article/who-cut-ukraines-starlink-speeds-musk-and-the-white-house-offer-conflicting-accounts-185435059.html

item.title: Social Security corrects millions of records. Could your benefits be affected?
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The U.S. Social Security Administration (SSA) said Tuesday that it has corrected millions of records associated with nearly 15% of active Social Security numbers (SSN), which it said was part of an effort to prevent fraud. The agency called it the "most comprehensive SSN record clean-up" in its 91-year history, and said it had added 17 million missing dates of death to its records and updated citizenship information for about 25 million records. It is also working to correct another 8.5 million records with inaccurate citizenship status and has introduced stronger internal controls to prevent future data-entry errors. "This is the first time SSA has undertaken an effort of this scale, and I am proud of the work we have done to strengthen the foundation of identity data relied upon throughout government and the economy," Commissioner Frank J. Bisignano said in a statement outlining the work the agency had carried out. The SSA said the changes are intended to improve the accuracy of records used by federal and state agencies to verify identities, prevent fraud and ensure government benefits are paid correctly. Here's what we know about the cleanup so far — and what it could mean for your account. What exactly has Social Security changed? The SSA cleanup focuses on the Social Security number (SSN) database, which government agencies use to verify identities and help administer benefits. According to the SSA , millions of records were missing a date of death or citizenship information. To address those gaps, the agency used information from its own systems and the State Department to add missing dates of death. It also used data from the Department of Homeland Security to update citizenship records. The SSA said the corrections are intended to improve the accuracy of its records, prevent fraud and reduce improper payments across government programs. The agency has also introduced stronger internal controls designed to prevent future errors caused by manual data entry. Could the cleanup affect your benefits or records? Accurate death and citizenship records help determine who is eligible for Social Security benefits and prevent incorrect payments. Death records are particularly important for survivor benefits, which provide financial support to eligible family members after someone receiving or eligible for Social Security dies. However, the SSA has not said whether its latest corrections have changed anyone's benefit payments or eligibility, or whether anyone has had problems with their records. The accuracy of death records has drawn scrutiny before. Earlier this year, a former senior SSA official alleged in a whistleblower disclosure that Homeland Security officials, with involvement from Department of Government Efficiency staff, pushed the agency to mark as many as 2.7 million people as dead without sufficient evidence. The former official said the plan was rejected but alleged that more than 6,000 people were incorrectly recorded as dead in a separate April 2025 update. The SSA has denied adding the proposed 2.7 million names to its Death Master File. Do you need to check your Social Security information? The SSA has not announced any new requirements for people to check or update their Social Security information after the cleanup. However, people can review some of their information through their online my Social Security account , including their earnings history and, for those receiving benefits, payment details. Anyone who notices an error in their records or experiences an unexpected interruption to their benefits can contact Social Security directly to ask about the issue and how to resolve it. The agency has not said that the latest cleanup requires beneficiaries to submit new documents or take any other action.
